lines.text: * These data structures are realloc'd when they grow, and the macro

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: "functions" write to the provided pointer. This means: (a) the pointer

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: must be an lvalue, and (b) the pointer to the data structure is not

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: stable, and you must maintain it the same as you would a realloc'd

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: pointer. For example, if you pass a pointer to a dynamic array to a

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: function which updates it, the function must return back the new

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: pointer to the caller. This is the price of trying to do this in C.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * The following are the only functions that are thread-safe on a single data

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: structure, i.e. can be run in multiple threads simultaneously on the same

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * You iterate over the contents of a dynamic array and a hashmap in exactly

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * All operations except arrins/arrdel are O(1) amortized, but individual

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: operations can be slow, so these data structures may not be suitable

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: for real time use. Dynamic arrays double in capacity as needed, so

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: elements are copied an average of once. Hash tables double/halve

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: their size as needed, with appropriate hysteresis to maintain O(1)

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * If you know how long a dynamic array is going to be in advance, you can avoid

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: extra memory allocations by using arrsetlen to allocate it to that length in

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: advance and use foo[n] while filling it out, or arrsetcap to allocate the memory

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: for that length and use arrput/arrpush as normal.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * Unlike some other versions of the dynamic array, this version should

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: be safe to use with strict-aliasing optimizations.

lines.author: matemolnar8

lines.text: Extensions are used that eliminate this requirement if you're using C99 and later

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: in GCC or clang, or if you're using C++ in GCC. But note that this can make your

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * To test for presence of a key in a hashmap, just do 'hmgeti(foo,key) >= 0'.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * The iteration order of your data in the hashmap is determined solely by the

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: order of insertions and deletions. In particular, if you never delete, new

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: keys are always added at the end of the array. This will be consistent

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: across all platforms and versions of the library. However, you should not

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: attempt to serialize the internal hash table, as the hash is not consistent

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: between different platforms, and may change with future versions of the library.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: * Use sh_new_arena() for string hashmaps that you never delete from. Initialize

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: with NULL if you're managing the memory for your strings, or your strings are

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: never freed (at least until the hashmap is freed). Otherwise, use sh_new_strdup().
